title: Malachi: turn the hearts (Malachi 3:23–24)
hook: the last prophet: Elijah will turn parents' hearts to children, children's to parents

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah's golden lamp, fed by two olive trees, and a message for a weary builder. Your line was not by might. What did you solve gently? Today, the last book of the Twelve, and its last lines. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

After all of it, the burning coal on Isaiah's lips, Jeremiah's broken jar, the valley of dry bones, Jonah in the sea, the books of the prophets end with a handful of short verses at the close of Malachi. First, a look back. In the King James: "Remember ye the law of Moses my servant." Then a look ahead: Elijah the prophet will be sent, before the great and terrible day of the LORD. And then the very last promise in the prophets. Of everything a prophet could hold out at the end, a rebuilt kingdom, defeated enemies, a world made new, Malachi chooses something much closer to home.
screen: `REMEMBER THE LAW OF MOSES.` → `ELIJAH WILL BE SENT.` → `THE LAST PROMISE IS CLOSE TO HOME.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." Read it once more and listen for the direction. It runs both ways. The Torah had already told children to honor their parents. This goes further. Parents turn too, and the parents are named first. Elijah's job, at the edge of the great day, isn't to win a battle. It's to get two generations facing each other again. Readers hear that in different ways. Some hear parents and children who've stopped understanding each other, and a promise that the gap will close. Some hear the generations of a people, the old ones who remember and the young ones who will carry it on, turned back toward the same Torah Malachi just told them to remember. It's the same Elijah who stood on Mount Carmel and went up in a whirlwind, and the same Elijah Jews welcome with a cup at the Passover table and sing about as Shabbat ends. Now, the hard part. The verse doesn't stop there. It goes on: turn the hearts, or the land will be struck with destruction. That's the last word of the book. And here's a custom. When Malachi is read aloud in synagogue, the reader doesn't stop on that harsh line. The custom is to go back and read the verse before it again, the promise of Elijah, so the prophets close on hope rather than ruin. Even in the reading, someone turns back toward the listener.
screen: `IT RUNS BOTH WAYS.` · `PARENTS ARE NAMED FIRST.` · then, large: `THE HEART OF THE FATHERS TO THE CHILDREN.` · then: `READ THE PROMISE AGAIN, END ON HOPE.`

segments.voice: Now the practice: reach across a generation. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone a generation away from you, older or younger. A parent or grandparent. A child, a niece, a nephew. An older neighbor, a young coworker. Notice whether your heart is turned toward them, or a little away. Then find one question you've never asked them about their life. What was hard at your age? What do you wish someone had told you? What are you into lately? Hold the question, and their face, for a while. If you pray, you can say Malachi's line with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Malachi. The last book of the Twelve, which closes the prophets with Elijah turning the hearts of parents and children toward each other. Today's word.
Your line: turn the hearts. Today, reach one generation over: ask your question, and let the answer run longer than you planned. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Malachi's closing verses are read in synagogue as a prophetic reading, including on the Shabbat before Passover, and by custom the verse promising Elijah is read again so the reading ends on hope.
